_comment: Sacred-scripture levels 16-18: real objections answered, the conquest narratives objection, historical-critical method/schools

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'The Bible gets a scientific or historical detail wrong somewhere, so it can't be inspired.' Using Dei Verbum 11's precise formula, what is the accurate response?
choices: Inerrancy applies to the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation, not necessarily to every incidental scientific or historical detail a text happens to mention
The objection is correct, and the Church has quietly abandoned any claim to inerrancy
Inerrancy means every single statement in Scripture must be scientifically precise by modern standards
The objection can only be answered by denying that the Bible mentions any historical events at all
questions.correctAnswer: Inerrancy applies to the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation, not necessarily to every incidental scientific or historical detail a text happens to mention
questions.explanation: Level 6 already fixed this precise formula: Dei Verbum locates inerrancy in the saving truth God wanted conveyed, not in a modern textbook's standard of precision for every incidental detail -- an ancient author's phenomenological description of the natural world, for instance, isn't a scientific claim the text is staking its inspired status on.
questions.hint: Inerrancy is located in the saving truth God wanted conveyed, not in a modern standard of scientific or historical precision for every incidental detail.

citations.quote: The books of Scripture firmly, faithfully, and without error teach the truth that God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to be put in writing in Holy Writ.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'Catholics added seven books to the Bible.' Using the canon history from level 6, what is the accurate reframing of this claim?
choices: The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon in the 16th century; Trent's 1546 session formally reaffirmed the longer list the Church had already used, rather than the Church adding anything new
The claim is entirely accurate exactly as stated -- the Catholic Church added the books at the Council of Trent
Neither Catholics nor Protestants have ever had a fixed Old Testament canon
The seven books in question were written after the New Testament closed
questions.correctAnswer: The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon in the 16th century; Trent's 1546 session formally reaffirmed the longer list the Church had already used, rather than the Church adding anything new
questions.explanation: The historical direction runs the opposite way from the objection: these books were already part of the Church's received and liturgically used canon well before the Reformation. Trent's Fourth Session formally reaffirmed that existing longer list in response to 16th-century Reformers removing these books, rather than the Church newly adding them.
questions.hint: This is a direction-of-history problem -- ask which side actually changed an existing, received list.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'The Gospels copied each other, so they aren't independent eyewitness testimony.' Using Markan priority and the Church's three-stage Gospel formation process (CCC 126), what is the accurate response?
choices: Literary dependence in composition and apostolic reliability in content aren't in tension -- later evangelists drawing on earlier written and oral apostolic tradition is exactly the process CCC 126 describes, not a discovery that undermines it
The Gospels have no literary relationship of any kind, and the extensive verbal overlap among the Synoptics is entirely coincidental rather than a sign of shared sources
The fact that later evangelists drew on earlier written material proves the Gospels are literary fiction rather than testimony rooted in apostolic memory
CCC 126 was written specifically to deny Markan priority and to rule out any use of one Gospel as a source for another
questions.correctAnswer: Literary dependence in composition and apostolic reliability in content aren't in tension -- later evangelists drawing on earlier written and oral apostolic tradition is exactly the process CCC 126 describes, not a discovery that undermines it
questions.explanation: CCC 126 describes a three-stage formation process -- the life and teaching of Jesus, the apostles' oral preaching, and the evangelists' later written composition drawing on those earlier stages. Mark being used as a source by Matthew and Luke is exactly this kind of continuity with apostolic tradition, not evidence of fabrication or independent invention.
questions.hint: The three-stage process in CCC 126 already accounts for later written Gospels drawing on earlier apostolic material.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: A sola scriptura objection claims, 'The Bible alone is a sufficient and self-interpreting rule of faith, with no need for the Church's authority.' Using the interpretive criteria already covered in this topic (living Tradition, the analogy of faith), what is the accurate response?
choices: Scripture itself requires correct interpretation within the living Tradition and the analogy of faith -- a text that different readers interpret in contradictory ways cannot function as a wholly self-interpreting rule without an authoritative interpreter
The Church agrees Scripture is entirely self-interpreting and needs no additional guidance whatsoever
The analogy of faith and living Tradition are modern Catholic inventions with no basis in how the earliest Christians read Scripture
Sola scriptura is correct, and the Catholic Church has quietly adopted it since Vatican II
questions.correctAnswer: Scripture itself requires correct interpretation within the living Tradition and the analogy of faith -- a text that different readers interpret in contradictory ways cannot function as a wholly self-interpreting rule without an authoritative interpreter
questions.explanation: The historical fact of thousands of different, mutually contradictory interpretations arising from sola scriptura is itself evidence against the claim that Scripture is simply self-interpreting -- the Church's teaching is that Scripture must be read within the living Tradition and 'analogy of faith' (the coherence of all revealed truths with each other), guided by the Magisterium's authority to interpret authentically.
questions.hint: The strongest evidence against 'self-interpreting' is simply how many contradictory readings the same text has actually produced.

citations.quote: Read the Scripture within 'the living Tradition of the whole Church'... it is the Holy Spirit who gives her the spiritual interpretation of the Scripture.

questions.prompt: True or False: The apparent tension between James 2:24 ('a person is justified by works and not by faith alone') and Romans 3:28 ('a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law') is resolved by recognizing the two authors use 'faith' and 'works' in different senses suited to the specific errors each is correcting, not by declaring one passage simply wrong.
questions.explanation: Paul in Romans is countering a reliance on the Mosaic law's ritual works as a means of justification apart from faith in Christ, while James is countering an empty, inert 'faith' that produces no actual charity or good works -- read according to each author's specific target and literary context, the two passages address different errors rather than contradicting each other.
questions.hint: The key move is asking what specific error each author is actually correcting, not assuming both must use the same word the same way.

citations.quote: For we consider that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
See how a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

questions.prompt: Match each objection to its accurate response.

pairs.left: 'The Bible gets a scientific detail wrong'
pairs.right: Inerrancy covers the saving truth God intended, not every incidental detail
The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon; Trent reaffirmed it
Literary dependence and apostolic reliability aren't in tension -- CCC 126's own three-stage process

pairs.left: 'The Bible alone is a sufficient, self-interpreting rule of faith'
pairs.right: Contradictory readings from the same text argue against 'self-interpreting' without the Church's authoritative interpretation

questions.explanation: Each of these responses draws on vocabulary and history already fixed at level 6 -- this level's whole task is putting that vocabulary to work against a real objection, not introducing new facts.
questions.hint: None of these four correct answers is a bare denial -- each engages the objection's actual claim.

citations.quote: Read the Scripture within 'the living Tradition of the whole Church'... it is the Holy Spirit who gives her the spiritual interpretation of the Scripture.

questions.prompt: An objector says: 'The Gospels contradict each other on small details, like the exact wording of the inscription over the cross, so they can't be trusted at all.'  What is the accurate response?
choices: Minor variation in incidental detail among independent witnesses is normal and does not undermine agreement on the substantial facts; ancient historians did not expect verbatim uniformity
The Gospels never differ on any detail whatsoever
The differences prove the events never happened
Only one Gospel's account of the inscription should be considered accurate, and the others are simply wrong
questions.correctAnswer: Minor variation in incidental detail among independent witnesses is normal and does not undermine agreement on the substantial facts; ancient historians did not expect verbatim uniformity
questions.explanation: Four independent witnesses to the same event nearly always vary slightly on incidental wording while agreeing on substance — a total absence of such variation would actually be more suspicious, suggesting collusion rather than independent testimony.
questions.hint: Ask what perfectly identical wording across four independent accounts would actually suggest.

questions.prompt: An objector claims: 'The Gospel of Mark ends abruptly at 16:8 with the women afraid, so the Resurrection appearances must be later additions with no basis.'  How should this be addressed?
choices: Mark's abrupt original ending is a real textual question addressed on its own terms in level 10 of this topic, and does not affect the independent, earlier attestation of the Resurrection in Paul's letters
Mark 16:9-20 is universally accepted as certainly original with no scholarly dispute
The claim proves the Resurrection was invented after Mark was written
This detail has no bearing on the reliability of any other Gospel
questions.correctAnswer: Mark's abrupt original ending is a real textual question addressed on its own terms in level 10 of this topic, and does not affect the independent, earlier attestation of the Resurrection in Paul's letters
questions.explanation: This is a genuine textual-critical question, not a threat to the Resurrection's attestation — 1 Corinthians 15, written earlier than Mark, already contains a creedal formula naming the Resurrection and witnesses, independent of how Mark's Gospel happens to end.
questions.hint: Ask whether the earliest evidence for the Resurrection depends on Mark's ending specifically.

questions.prompt: True or False: The apparent tension between James 2:24 ('a person is justified by works and not by faith alone') and Paul's teaching on justification by faith is resolved by recognizing they are answering different questions about faith.
questions.explanation: True. James addresses a faith that is mere intellectual assent producing no fruit — dead faith — while Paul addresses whether observance of the Mosaic Law's works earns justification. They are not contradicting each other on the same question; they are answering two different questions the word 'faith' can raise.
questions.hint: Ask whether 'works' and 'faith' mean exactly the same thing in each author's argument.

questions.prompt: Match each objection to its accurate response.

pairs.left: 'The Gospels contradict each other on small details'
pairs.right: Normal variation among independent witnesses on incidental detail
A real textual question, unrelated to Paul's earlier, independent attestation
Different questions about faith, not a real contradiction
Genuinely disputed passages like this one show interpretation needs more than the text alone

questions.explanation: The fourth row uses this very level's own material as its evidence: real, sincere disagreement among readers of James and Paul over centuries is itself a demonstration that the text alone did not settle every dispute, which is exactly the sola scriptura difficulty covered elsewhere in this database.
questions.hint: One row uses the disagreement discussed in this level as evidence for a larger point about biblical interpretation.

questions.prompt: An objector says: 'The Old Testament's conquest narratives, where Israel is commanded to destroy entire peoples, show the Bible actually endorses real, genocidal violence.' What is the real, first, careful move in answering this genuinely serious real objection?
choices: Taking the real, historical genre seriously -- ancient conquest accounts used hyperbolic 'total destruction' language, not always literal
Simply dismissing the objection as unworthy of any real, serious response
Conceding immediately that the Bible does, in fact, straightforwardly endorse real, literal genocide with no further real distinction needed
Refusing to actually read or engage the real, specific biblical texts being raised in the objection
questions.correctAnswer: Taking the real, historical genre seriously -- ancient conquest accounts used hyperbolic 'total destruction' language, not always literal
questions.explanation: This is a real, serious objection deserving a real, careful, first move -- attending to genre, exactly as this topic's own earlier level established. Ancient Near Eastern conquest accounts conventionally used real, hyperbolic 'total destruction' language that the biblical text's own later real references (showing the same peoples still present) confirm was not always literal.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own earlier level on why genre actually matters for reading any passage well.

questions.prompt: True or False: Later biblical texts sometimes refer to peoples the conquest narratives describe as totally destroyed as still actually present, suggesting the destruction language functioned rhetorically rather than as a literal, complete historical record.
questions.explanation: True, and this is a real, important piece of real, internal biblical evidence -- later texts referring to supposedly 'totally destroyed' peoples as still actually present shows the destruction language functioned as a real, conventional rhetorical device, not a strictly literal historical claim.
questions.hint: Consider what it would mean if a people described as 'totally destroyed' shows up again, still present, later in the same real biblical narrative.

questions.prompt: Beyond the real, genre-based answer, why does the Church also insist inerrancy concerns the real, saving truth God wanted communicated, not every real, incidental historical detail or ancient cultural assumption?
choices: An ancient cultural context reflected in the narrative isn't God's own moral endorsement of every real, described action
Because this distinction actually has no real bearing on the conquest narratives specifically
Because inerrancy actually requires treating every real, described action in Scripture as morally endorsed by God
Because the Church has never actually addressed this specific real question at all
questions.correctAnswer: An ancient cultural context reflected in the narrative isn't God's own moral endorsement of every real, described action
questions.explanation: This applies this topic's own earlier real distinction directly -- inerrancy's own real, saving truth does not mean every real, described action or ancient cultural assumption reflected in the narrative is thereby God's own positive, moral endorsement of it.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own earlier level distinguishing inerrancy's real, saving truth from every incidental detail.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own two-part real answer -- genre and the real scope of inerrancy -- draws directly on tools this topic already built in its own earlier levels.
questions.explanation: True, and naming this connection matters -- this level does not introduce a wholly new real method; it applies this topic's own earlier real tools (genre, the precise scope of inerrancy) to a genuinely serious, real, further objection.
questions.hint: Consider what real tools this level's own two-part answer actually drew on from earlier in this topic.

questions.prompt: A skeptic pushes further: 'Even a rhetorical exaggeration is still troubling -- why would God even permit this kind of violent language in Scripture at all?' What is the real, honest, careful response?
choices: This remains genuinely hard, and honest, ongoing engagement respects the real difficulty rather than a quick, dismissive answer
There is actually no real, hard question here at all, and any real, remaining discomfort is simply a sign of insufficient faith
This question should actually never be discussed or engaged by ordinary Catholics at all
The real, honest answer is that Scripture actually contains a straightforward real error at this specific point
questions.correctAnswer: This remains genuinely hard, and honest, ongoing engagement respects the real difficulty rather than a quick, dismissive answer
questions.explanation: This is a real, honest acknowledgment worth making directly -- some real, hard questions do not resolve into a single, tidy, dismissive answer; honest, ongoing, careful engagement respects the real difficulty rather than pretending it away, following the same real intellectual honesty this topic has practiced throughout.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own repeated real emphasis on honest engagement rather than convenient, dismissive answers.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real honesty about a genuinely hard, unresolved question follows the same real pattern this app's own Apologetics topic modeled when it honestly acknowledged Mark's longer ending lacked early manuscript support.
questions.explanation: True, and naming this shared real method matters -- both levels practice the same underlying real discipline: honest, careful engagement with a genuinely hard real question, rather than a convenient, dismissive answer.
questions.hint: Recall this app's own Apologetics topic's level on honestly engaging an inconvenient real finding.

pairs.right: Conventionally used hyperbolic 'total destruction' language, not always literal
Real, internal biblical evidence the language functioned rhetorically
Ancient cultural context reflected in a text is not God's own moral endorsement of it

pairs.left: This remaining a genuinely hard question
pairs.right: Honest, ongoing engagement, not a quick, dismissive resolution

questions.explanation: These four facts together model this topic's own real, honest method for a genuinely serious objection -- careful, multi-part reasoning, without pretending every real difficulty simply disappears.
questions.hint: Three rows build the real, careful answer; one names this level's own real, honest limit.

questions.prompt: True or False: Having now answered a further, genuinely serious real objection, this topic's next level turns to historical-critical method and real interpretive schools.
questions.explanation: True. Having modeled real, honest, careful engagement with a genuinely hard objection, this topic's next level turns to the real, formal methods scholars actually use to study Scripture's own historical dimension.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: What real, general habit has this level modeled for engaging a genuinely serious, difficult real objection to Scripture?
choices: Applying earlier tools carefully while honestly naming remaining real difficulty, not forcing a tidy resolution
Dismissing the objection outright as unworthy of any real, serious engagement
Conceding the objection entirely without offering any real, careful response
Pretending a genuinely hard real question has already been completely and simply resolved
questions.correctAnswer: Applying earlier tools carefully while honestly naming remaining real difficulty, not forcing a tidy resolution
questions.explanation: This level's own real habit -- careful reasoning combined with honest acknowledgment of remaining real difficulty -- is exactly the same real discipline this topic has practiced throughout, and will keep practicing through its own later levels.
questions.hint: Consider what this level actually did with a genuinely hard, real objection that does not resolve into an easy answer.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of honestly engaging a genuinely serious real objection, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Historical-critical method and real interpretive schools
A complete repeat of this same level's material about the conquest narratives
A jump ahead to typology and cross-topic connections, skipping over everything in between
A subject entirely unrelated to Scripture or its own real, difficult questions
questions.correctAnswer: Historical-critical method and real interpretive schools
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers -- moving from a specific, hard objection to the real, formal methods scholars actually use to engage Scripture's own historical dimension carefully.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: Per Dei Verbum 12 and the Pontifical Biblical Commission's 1993 document 'The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church,' what is the historical-critical method's legitimate contribution, and what is its limit when used alone?
choices: It legitimately illuminates authorial intent and historical/literary context, but risks missing a text's full theological meaning if it excludes the light of faith and Tradition
It has no legitimate use in Catholic biblical scholarship and is formally condemned
It fully replaces the need for any theological or spiritual reading of Scripture
It applies only to the New Testament, never to the Old Testament
questions.correctAnswer: It legitimately illuminates authorial intent and historical/literary context, but risks missing a text's full theological meaning if it excludes the light of faith and Tradition
questions.explanation: The 1993 PBC document affirms the historical-critical method's real, positive contribution to understanding a text's original context and intended meaning, while cautioning that used in isolation -- without the complementary light of faith, Tradition, and the Church's living interpretation -- it risks missing dimensions of meaning Dei Verbum 12 says belong to a text inspired by God for the Church's ongoing life.
questions.hint: This is a 'legitimate but incomplete alone' answer, not a flat approval or rejection.

citations.quote: The interpreter must investigate what meaning the sacred writer intended to express and actually expressed in particular circumstances by using contemporary literary forms.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Alexandrian school's emphasis on allegory and the Antiochene school's emphasis on literal-historical restraint represent two legitimate but different accents within the same fourfold-sense framework, not a simple right-versus-wrong pair.
questions.explanation: Both schools operated within the Church's broader tradition of reading Scripture according to multiple senses (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical); Alexandria leaned toward drawing out the allegorical and typological, while Antioch leaned toward historical and grammatical restraint -- legitimate differences of emphasis, not one school being simply orthodox and the other simply in error.
questions.hint: This is a difference of emphasis within a shared framework, similar to other legitimate diversities already seen in this app.

citations.quote: one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: Given the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), which correctly matches a historical-critical reading to its characteristic concern, as distinct from an allegorical reading's concern?
choices: Historical-critical: the passage's ancient Near Eastern context and the practice of child sacrifice it stands against; allegorical: Isaac as a type of Christ carrying wood to his own sacrifice
Historical-critical and allegorical readings ask exactly the same question and reach exactly the same conclusion
Historical-critical readings are concerned only with allegory; allegorical readings are concerned only with historical context
Neither reading has any legitimate basis in Catholic biblical scholarship
questions.correctAnswer: Historical-critical: the passage's ancient Near Eastern context and the practice of child sacrifice it stands against; allegorical: Isaac as a type of Christ carrying wood to his own sacrifice
questions.explanation: A historical-critical reading situates the passage against its ancient Near Eastern background, noting how it stands against child sacrifice practiced by surrounding cultures; an allegorical/typological reading, already licensed by the fourfold-sense framework, sees Isaac carrying the wood for his own sacrifice as prefiguring Christ carrying his cross -- both are legitimate readings operating at different levels of the text's meaning.
questions.hint: One reading looks outward to ancient context; the other looks forward to how the passage prefigures Christ.

citations.quote: We can acquire a more profound understanding of events by recognizing their significance in Christ; thus the crossing of the Red Sea is a sign or type of Christ's victory and also of Christian Baptism.

questions.prompt: The Documentary Hypothesis proposes that the Pentateuch was compiled from four source traditions (J, E, D, P) rather than written entirely by Moses alone. Per the Pontifical Biblical Commission's 1948 letter to Cardinal Suhard, what is the Church's actual stance on this hypothesis?
choices: It is permitted as a legitimate scholarly hypothesis for Catholic exegetes to discuss and weigh, not binding doctrine that must be accepted or rejected as a matter of faith
It has been formally condemned as heretical
It has been formally declared the Church's official teaching on the Pentateuch's authorship
It applies only to the book of Genesis, not the rest of the Pentateuch
questions.correctAnswer: It is permitted as a legitimate scholarly hypothesis for Catholic exegetes to discuss and weigh, not binding doctrine that must be accepted or rejected as a matter of faith
questions.explanation: The 1948 PBC letter to Cardinal Suhard acknowledged the value of source-critical study of the Pentateuch's composition history while affirming Mosaic authorship in a broader, substantial sense (Moses as the tradition's authoritative source, even if later editors compiled and shaped the final text) -- treating the specific documentary details as an open scholarly question, not a matter the faith requires settling one way or the other.
questions.hint: This is the same pattern as level 6's point about disputed Pauline authorship -- a scholarly question the Church leaves open rather than dogmatically resolving.

citations.reference: Pontifical Biblical Commission, Letter to Cardinal Suhard (1948)

questions.prompt: True or False: Whether the Alexandrian or Antiochene emphasis best serves preaching today is a contested-within-orthodoxy methodological question, while the claim that Scripture has a literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical sense at all is settled Catholic teaching, not an open question.
questions.explanation: The fourfold-sense framework itself -- that Scripture bears these different levels of meaning -- is settled Catholic teaching (CCC 115-119); which historical school's emphasis is more pastorally useful for preaching in a given context is a live, legitimate methodological question, not a doctrinal one. Confusing the two would either wrongly dogmatize a preference or wrongly relativize a settled teaching.
questions.hint: One of these two claims is about whether something exists at all; the other is about which emphasis works best in practice.

citations.quote: one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: Match each method or school to its central working concern.

pairs.right: Authorial intent and historical/literary context
Literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical layers of meaning
An accent toward allegory and typology
An accent toward literal-historical restraint

questions.explanation: No single fact settles which method or school 'wins' at this level -- the task is matching each to its actual working concern, since several of these operate legitimately side by side rather than replacing one another.
questions.hint: Two of these are broad methods; two are specific historical schools within the patristic approach.

citations.quote: The interpreter must investigate what meaning the sacred writer intended to express and actually expressed in particular circumstances by using contemporary literary forms.

questions.prompt: According to Dei Verbum 12, what must an interpreter attend to alongside literary form and historical context when reading Scripture?
choices: The content and unity of Scripture as a whole, and the living Tradition of the Church
Only the original autograph manuscripts, none of which survive
Only a single Church Father's interpretation, treated as final
Contemporary popular opinion about the passage's meaning
questions.correctAnswer: The content and unity of Scripture as a whole, and the living Tradition of the Church
questions.explanation: Dei Verbum 12 explicitly requires reading historical-critical findings together with the whole of Scripture and the Church's living Tradition — the historical method is genuinely valued, but never treated as sufficient on its own, apart from the Church's ongoing interpretive life.
questions.hint: The document names two things beyond historical method itself that interpretation must attend to.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Alexandrian school's emphasis on allegory and the Antiochene school's emphasis on literal-historical reading were simply incompatible, with the Church eventually declaring one wrong.
questions.explanation: False. Both schools contributed genuine insight, and the Church has never condemned either emphasis wholesale — she draws on the literal grounding the Antiochenes stressed and the christological depth the Alexandrians pursued, which is exactly why the Catechism's four senses of Scripture include both a literal and several spiritual senses rather than picking one school over the other.
questions.hint: Ask whether the Catechism's own senses of Scripture, covered earlier in this topic, favor only one of these emphases.

questions.prompt: Given the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), which correctly matches a historical-critical reading to a typological reading, without setting the two against each other?
choices: Historically, the narrative reflects ancient Israel's rejection of child sacrifice; typologically, it foreshadows the Father offering his own Son, who (unlike Isaac) is not spared
The historical-critical reading proves the typological reading false
Only the typological reading is theologically acceptable; the historical reading should be discarded
The two readings address identical questions and cannot both be held
questions.correctAnswer: Historically, the narrative reflects ancient Israel's rejection of child sacrifice; typologically, it foreshadows the Father offering his own Son, who (unlike Isaac) is not spared
questions.explanation: These are two different, complementary levels of reading the same text: one asks what the passage meant in its ancient Near Eastern context, the other asks how the same passage points forward to Christ. Neither displaces the other, and holding both is exactly what CCC 128-130 does with this narrative.
questions.hint: Ask whether a historical reading and a typological reading have to compete, or can both be true at once.

questions.prompt: Match each method or school to its central working concern.

pairs.right: The text's original historical and literary context
Allegorical depth, Christ present throughout the text
Literal-historical grounding before spiritual reading
Proposes four source traditions compiled into the Pentateuch

questions.explanation: None of these approaches is, by itself, the Church's whole method of reading Scripture — each contributes one genuine concern, and Dei Verbum 12's own instruction is to hold historical method together with unity and Tradition rather than let any one approach stand alone.
questions.hint: Ask what specific concern each method or school contributes, without assuming any one of them is sufficient alone.
